passage:
12 March, night
Went to Sharmila's home today for the thirteenth-day prayers for her father. I'd never been to one. Cousins were rolling puris in the courtyard, someone had put his reading glasses beside the photo, and everyone ate together on long mats. It felt like the whole lane was holding the family up.
But I also heard an aunt tell Sharmila, "Be strong, beta, don't cry in front of the guests." Sharmila nodded and went completely still after that, as if she'd left the room without moving.
Later an old neighbour sat with her and asked, "What was he like on Sunday mornings?" Sharmila laughed, then cried, then told us about his terrible puns. Nobody rushed her.
I'm her colleague, not family, and I don't know the right words. But tomorrow I'll send her one of his puns and ask how she's doing.
Ayesha

qa.q: What had someone put beside the photo?
qa.a: His reading glasses.

qa.q: What does Sharmila going completely still suggest about how she felt after the aunt spoke?
qa.a: It suggests she felt she had to hide her grief and pulled into herself, alone even in a full house.

qa.q: What did Ayesha decide to do tomorrow, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: To send Sharmila one of her father's puns and ask how she is, which invites her to speak of him without being hurried.

qa.q: How did the neighbour's question change things for Sharmila?
qa.a: Being asked what her father was like let her laugh, cry and share his puns, so she felt accompanied instead of told to be strong.

grounding: It shows a colleague at thirteenth-day prayers seeing shared meals hold a family up, and noticing that being told to be strong silences the mourner while gentle questions help.

passage:
Jahnavi: How was today? Thinking of you.
Zeenat: Full house. Neighbours have sent food every day since Nani passed. Nobody has cooked in our kitchen for a week.
Jahnavi: That sounds like a lot of people holding you all.
Zeenat: It is. The prayer gathering was nice. Everyone shared one memory of her.
Zeenat: But Chachu keeps saying "Be strong, you're the eldest grandchild." So I cry in the bathroom.
Jahnavi: You don't have to be strong with me.
Jahnavi: What memory did you share?
Zeenat: That she cheated at ludo and denied it every single time.
Zeenat: Sorry, long message coming.
Jahnavi: Take your time. I'm not going anywhere.
Jahnavi read the last line twice, put the kettle on and kept the chat open on her lap.

qa.q: Since when have neighbours sent food?
qa.a: Every day since Nani passed.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi seem to feel after reading Zeenat's messages, and what shows it?
qa.a: She seems caring and concerned for Zeenat; she reads the last line twice, puts the kettle on and keeps the chat open on her lap.

qa.q: Which reply from Jahnavi opened the conversation up, and why?
qa.a: "You don't have to be strong with me", followed by asking about a memory, because it let Zeenat grieve and speak of Nani without being hurried.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel reading "Take your time. I'm not going anywhere"?
qa.a: Zeenat may feel less alone and free to write the long message without rushing.

grounding: It shows an observer of mourning seeing neighbours' meals and shared memories give structure to loss, while a call to be strong pushes the mourner to cry alone.

passage: On the thirteenth day after Gurpreet's father died, the whole village gathered at the gurdwara for the bhog. Yogesh, twenty-five, their neighbour since childhood, sat at the back and watched. Two aunties kept telling Gurpreet, "Be strong, don't cry, he's with Waheguru." Each time, she pressed her lips tight and looked away. After the prayers, in the langar hall, Yogesh sat down next to her with his plate. "Your father taught me to ride a cycle on this very road. He ran behind me shouting." Gurpreet laughed, then cried openly. Yogesh just let her. She told him three more stories. When she stood to serve dal, her shoulders had loosened.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet's father teach Yogesh?
qa.a: He taught Yogesh to ride a cycle on the village road.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel watching the aunties tell Gurpreet to be strong?
qa.a: He seemed uneasy and concerned, noticing that their words made her hold back her tears.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do that supported Gurpreet's grief?
qa.a: He sat with her at the shared meal, spoke about her father, let her cry and listened without hurrying her.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt when the aunties said "Be strong"?
qa.a: She likely felt pressured and alone, pressing her lips tight and looking away instead of grieving openly.

grounding: Shows an observer at a community rite and shared meal who lets a mourner cry and speak of her father, unlike those who tell her to be strong.

passage: After the funeral in Oslo, everyone gathered in the church hall for coffee and cake, as they always did. Jin, twenty-four, had worked beside Anders for two years and came to support him. A cousin clapped Anders on the back. "Stay strong, eh? She wouldn't want tears." Anders nodded stiffly and stared into his cup. Jin waited until the cousin moved away. "Tell me about your mother's garden. You always talked about her roses." Anders was quiet. Then he started: the yellow ones by the fence, how she'd make him carry manure. His voice broke, and he cried. Jin didn't say anything to fix it. He just stayed, refilling Anders's coffee when it went cold.

qa.q: What did everyone have in the church hall?
qa.a: They had coffee and cake.

qa.q: How did Jin feel when the cousin told Anders to stay strong?
qa.a: He seemed uncomfortable and quietly concerned, waiting for a chance to let Anders talk.

qa.q: What did Jin do that helped Anders grieve?
qa.a: He invited Anders to speak about his mother's garden, let him cry and stayed without trying to fix it.

qa.q: How might Anders have felt when told she wouldn't want tears?
qa.a: Anders likely felt shut down and alone, nodding stiffly instead of expressing his grief.

grounding: Shows an observer at a funeral gathering who lets a grieving colleague speak of his mother and cry, unlike those who urge him to be strong.

passage: The office held a small prayer meeting in the conference room for Kalyani's brother, who had died in an accident. There were garlands, a photo and sweets afterwards. Alka, twenty-six, watched from the side. Their manager said to Kalyani, "Be strong. Come back fully on Monday, it'll help to be busy." Kalyani nodded and went very quiet. At lunch she sat alone. Alka carried her tiffin over. "What was your brother like?" Kalyani blinked. "He used to call me every night at nine, just to tell me a bad joke." She laughed, and then her face crumpled. Alka stayed, letting her cry into her dupatta. "Tell me the worst joke," she said. Kalyani did.

qa.q: What time did Kalyani's brother call her every night?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: How did Alka feel watching the manager speak to Kalyani?
qa.a: Alka seemed concerned, noticing that the manager's words made Kalyani go quiet and withdraw.

qa.q: What did Alka do that supported Kalyani?
qa.a: She sat with her at lunch, asked about her brother, let her laugh and cry and did not hurry her.

qa.q: How might Kalyani have felt being told to be strong and come back fully?
qa.a: She may have felt isolated and rushed, as if her grief wasn't welcome at work.

grounding: Shows an observer at a workplace prayer meeting who lets a mourner speak of her brother and cry, unlike a manager who tells her to be strong.

passage:
Dear Amma,
I got back from Salma's home in Malappuram last night. I wanted to tell you about it.
When her father died, the whole street came. Neighbours cooked for three days; nobody let the family light their stove. The men and women prayed, and people sat with them for hours, just being there.
But some relatives kept telling Salma, "Be strong. Don't cry in front of your mother." Each time, she went stiff and quiet. I watched her sit alone in the back room.
Then her old aunt came in, sat beside her and said, "Tell me about the time your father fell in the pond." Salma laughed and then cried properly, for the first time. The aunt just held her.
I did what the aunt did. I asked about him. I didn't hurry her. I think it's the most useful thing I've done all year.
Your Lakshmi

qa.q: How many days did neighbours cook for Salma's family?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel watching Salma sit alone in the back room?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt sad and worried for Salma, noticing how the "be strong" comments seemed to isolate her.

qa.q: Which response helped Salma, and why?
qa.a: Her aunt's invitation to talk about her father, without hurrying her, let Salma laugh and cry, unlike the relatives who told her to be strong.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt when relatives told her not to cry?
qa.a: She probably felt lonely and shut in with her grief, going stiff and quiet and withdrawing to the back room.

grounding: Lakshmi observes how shared rites and meals give structure to Salma's loss, how "be strong" isolates her, and how letting her cry and speak of her father helps.
